analysis.one_liner: Requires utilities to sell a rising share of renewable electricity and meet energy-savings targets.
analysis.headline: Introduced in the House on December 18, 2020, with three sponsors, it was referred to committee and never received a hearing or vote before the Congress ended two weeks later.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a national standard requiring large electric utilities to get at least 21% of their electricity from renewable sources in 2021, rising to 55% by 2030 and further each year through 2039. It would also require large electric and natural gas utilities to hit cumulative energy-savings targets through efficiency programs, appliance standards, and building codes, with penalties for falling short. The bill died in committee without ever getting a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Households and businesses would benefit in two ways: the efficiency standard requires utilities to fund weatherization, better appliances, and building upgrades that cut energy bills, and the renewable standard shifts generation toward wind, solar, and other sources whose fuel is free, reducing exposure to fossil fuel price swings. Renewable electricity generators gain a guaranteed national market, with double credits for projects in communities hit by coal plant closures or pollution and on tribal land. Anyone breathing air downwind of fossil power plants would benefit from reduced emissions.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Households, clean-energy builders, and coal-affected communities

how_it_helps.text: Sets a federal renewable electricity standard requiring large utilities to hit 21% renewable sales in 2021, 55% by 2030, and roughly 4 percentage points more each year through 2039.

Requires large electric utilities to achieve cumulative electricity savings up to 22% and gas utilities up to 14% by 2035 through efficiency programs, appliance standards, and building codes, counting weatherization, insulation, and heating and cooling upgrades toward the targets.

Issues double credits for renewable generation in economically distressed communities affected by coal plant closures or pollution and on Indian land, and lets utilities pay $50 per missed credit into state funds that must be spent on renewable deployment or efficiency.
Preserves state authority to set stricter renewable requirements and clarifies that states can set rates for renewable energy production incentive programs.

analysis.who_pays: Fossil-fuel generators — coal and natural gas plant owners — would lose sales as utilities buy renewable credits instead. Electric and gas utilities would bear compliance and program costs, which they would seek to recover through rates, so some of the near-term cost would land on ratepayers, particularly in states with little renewable generation; a $50-per-credit alternative compliance payment caps the effective price of the mandate.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs would flow into utility rates, at least in the near term, and the bill encourages state regulators to let utilities recover program costs, lost margins from lower sales, and even shareholder incentive bonuses, so the savings do not automatically reach customers in full.

The $50 alternative compliance payment and the ability to bank credits for three years give utilities a relatively cheap way to pay rather than build, which could blunt the bill's intended renewable buildout.

Defining eligible resources is contested: the bill counts qualified hydropower added to existing dams, biomass meeting a lifecycle emissions test, and landfill gas, choices that environmental groups often dispute, and the efficiency standard's measurement-and-verification regime is complex and could reward paper savings.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's core trade is a modest, capped near-term rate impact for a mandated shift to cheaper-to-run renewable generation and utility-funded efficiency that directly lowers household bills. The strongest objection is not the goal but the plumbing: generous cost recovery for utilities and a low buy-out price could let compliance costs stick to ratepayers while the emissions benefits arrive slowly. On balance, if it had passed, most households would likely come out ahead on total energy costs over time, but the design left room for utility shareholders to capture more of the benefit than the text promised.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, two weeks before the session ended, and the committee never took it up.

narrative.text: Rep. Peter Welch introduced the bill on December 18, 2020, with Reps. Yvette Clarke and Ben Ray Luján as the only cosponsors.

The House referred it to the Committee on Energy and Commerce on the day of introduction, and the action history shows no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without action, fossil-fuel generators and utilities avoided a federal renewable mandate and efficiency obligations, and renewable developers lost a guaranteed national market. Households did not receive the bill's mandated bill-lowering efficiency programs, though existing state programs continued unaffected.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fossil generators and utilities avoided the mandate

for.name: Rep. Peter Welch
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill establishing a federal renewable electricity standard and federal efficiency standard.

for.name: Reps. Yvette Clarke and Ben Ray Luján
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; they were the only cosponsors listed.

against.name: Rep. Frank Pallone and the House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day of introduction and took no further action; no hearing, markup, or floor consideration occurred before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Only three members — all Democrats — sponsored or cosponsored the bill, and no vote was ever taken, so no partisan split can be measured from the record.

industries.industry: Renewable electricity generators (wind, solar, geothermal, landfill gas)
industries.note: The bill creates a national tradeable credit market with a rising mandate through 2039, guaranteeing demand for renewable generation, and awards double credits for projects in coal-affected or polluted communities and on tribal land. Households gain the cleaner power supply the mandate forces.

industries.industry: Coal and natural gas electricity generators
industries.note: As utilities meet the renewable target, fossil plants lose sales, and their output becomes the price-taker behind the credit obligation. Their interest in stopping the bill ran against the cleaner air and long-term price stability the mandate promised.

Utilities would be the permanent administrators of the efficiency standard — claiming savings, buying credits, and paying penalties — and the bill encourages regulators to let them recover program costs, lost margins, and shareholder incentive bonuses even as it regulates them. That locks in their gatekeeper role over both renewable compliance and ratepayer-funded efficiency.

Large gas utilities would face cumulative savings targets up to 14% by 2035 and $10-per-million-Btu penalties for shortfalls, cutting the volume of gas they sell. Efficiency savings would lower customers' bills, though, so the industry's loss overlaps with customer benefit.

industries.industry: Biomass, wood products, and hydropower operators
industries.note: The bill counts hydropower capacity added to existing dams and biomass meeting a 50%-better-than-gas lifecycle emissions test as qualifying renewables, opening the mandate's value to those industries. Whether those sources deliver real climate benefit was a point of contention the bill addressed only through EPA accounting guidelines.
